subject: EM
title: Natural resources
strategyIntro: Environmental Management has no Core or Extended split. The full exam is Paper 1 (theory: short questions, then longer questions using source material) and Paper 2 (management in context, based on one country). Most marks come from reading sources and building arguments.

strategy.title: Quote the data
points: Most marks come from graphs, tables and maps.
Use figures with units: “fell from 62% to 41%” scores; “it fell” doesn’t.
Describe the overall trend first, then give the highest, lowest or any exception.

strategy.title: The 6-mark argument
points: Usually one per paper: discuss a statement for and against.
Structure: two points for, two against, then a conclusion.
Each point needs a reason: say why it matters, not just what it is.

strategy.title: Use your case study
points: Name the mine and the country. Specific facts lift your mark.
On Paper 2, link every answer back to the country in the source. General answers score lower.

strategy.title: Fieldwork comes up every year
points: Know sampling, quadrats, questionnaires and how to make them reliable.
Evaluate a method: one strength, one weakness, one improvement.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
Weigh up both sides and finish with a judgement.

dataPractice.intro: Practise the skill that earns the most marks. Look at the chart, then answer each question quoting the figures.
dataPractice.chartTitle: Electricity generated by source, Country X (% of total)
dataPractice.flag: Made-up figures for practice. Each year adds up to 100%.

questions.q: Describe how the share of electricity generated from coal changed between 2005 and 2025.
points: Coal’s share decreased
From 62% in 2005 to 41% in 2025 / a fall of 21 percentage points
questions.note: The second mark needs the figures with %.

questions.q: Which energy source increased its share the most? Use figures in your answer.
points: Wind
Rose from 3% to 14% (11 percentage points)
questions.note: Solar rose 10 points (0% to 10%), so check carefully before answering.

questions.q: Calculate the percentage of electricity generated from renewable sources in 2025.
points: HEP + wind + solar = 11 + 14 + 10
questions.note: Nuclear is not renewable (uranium is finite), even though it is low-carbon.

questions.q: Suggest two reasons why the share of wind and solar power increased.
points: Government targets to cut carbon dioxide emissions / climate change agreements
Cost of solar panels and wind turbines has fallen
To reduce reliance on imported or finite fossil fuels (energy security)
Subsidies or grants for renewable energy
Concern about air pollution from burning coal

planner.intro: Plan two practice answers in the 2 + 2 + conclusion structure. Write each point as a short sentence with a reason, then compare with the model points.

statements.text: The benefits of opening a new open-pit mine outweigh the costs to the environment.
for: Creates jobs and income for local people
Brings infrastructure such as roads, electricity and water
Tax and export earnings for the government
against: Dust and noise from blasting and trucks
Water pollution from runoff and waste (spoil, tailings)
Visual impact of the pit and spoil heaps
Local communities may be moved off their land
statements.conclusion: The benefits can outweigh the costs only if the mine is well managed: an environmental impact assessment before work starts, strict pollution laws, and a plan to restore the land when mining ends.

statements.text: Countries should replace fossil fuels with renewable energy as quickly as possible.
for: Cuts carbon dioxide emissions, reducing climate change
Fossil fuels are finite and will run out
Less air pollution and acid rain from burning coal
Less reliance on imported fuel (energy security)
against: Wind and solar are intermittent, so storage or backup is needed
High start-up costs, hard for poorer countries
Jobs lost in coal mining and power stations
Some renewables have impacts too: HEP dams flood land and move people
statements.conclusion: Countries should switch as fast as they can afford, but gradually enough to keep a reliable supply and retrain workers, using a mix of sources rather than relying on one.

quizIntro: These are not exam-format questions (EM has no multiple choice). Use them to check the facts are secure before you try the longer questions.

options: Magma or lava cools and solidifies
Existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure
Rocks are broken down by weathering
quiz.why: Granite (cooled slowly underground, large crystals) and basalt (cooled quickly at the surface, small crystals).
Limestone and sandstone are sedimentary. Marble is metamorphic: limestone changed by heat and pressure.

options: Existing rocks are changed by heat and / or pressure without melting
Layers of sand are deposited in the sea
A rock containing enough of a mineral or metal to make extraction worthwhile
quiz.why: Whether a rock counts as an ore depends on how much metal it holds and the price of that metal.

options: The deposit is close to the surface
There is no overburden at all
quiz.why: The overburden (rock and soil on top) is removed to reach a shallow deposit. Deep deposits need shaft mining.

quiz.q: Which is an environmental impact of mining, not a social or economic one?
quiz.why: Habitat loss, dust, noise and water pollution are environmental. Jobs, roads and tax are social or economic benefits.

quiz.q: Which would make a mineral deposit LESS likely to be mined?
options: High world price for the mineral
Located in a protected national park
quiz.why: Other factors: low grade, great depth, high cost, low demand, poor access, strict environmental laws.

quiz.q: What is an environmental impact assessment (EIA)?
options: A report written after a mine closes
A study of the likely impacts of a project before it is approved
quiz.why: An EIA weighs up environmental, social and economic impacts before a decision is made.

quiz.q: Which of these is a way to restore land after mining?
quiz.why: Restoration also includes filling the pit, landscaping, or flooding it to make a lake for wildlife or recreation.

quiz.q: Why does recycling metals help manage resources sustainably?
options: It uses more energy than mining
It conserves a finite resource and needs less mining
quiz.why: Recycling also usually uses less energy than extracting new metal and reduces landfill.

options: Remains of plants and animals buried and compressed over millions of years
quiz.why: Coal from plants in swamps; oil and natural gas from tiny sea organisms. They are non-renewable.
Geothermal uses heat from inside the Earth, which will not run out. Uranium is finite.

quiz.q: A main disadvantage of wind power is that:
options: It releases lots of carbon dioxide
It only generates electricity when the wind blows
quiz.why: Wind and solar are intermittent. Some people also object to noise and the look of turbines.

quiz.q: A main disadvantage of hydroelectric power (HEP) is that:
options: Large areas of land are flooded behind the dam
quiz.why: Flooding destroys habitats and can force people to move. HEP is reliable and releases no CO₂ when running.

quiz.q: Which is an advantage of nuclear power?
options: Very low carbon dioxide emissions when generating
quiz.why: Disadvantages: radioactive waste dangerous for thousands of years, risk of accidents, high building and decommissioning costs.

quiz.q: Which is a way to reduce energy use in a home?
options: Fitting loft insulation and double glazing
quiz.why: Also: LED bulbs, efficient appliances, turning off devices, solar water heating.

flashIntro: Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: A naturally occurring solid with a definite chemical make-up.
Rock containing enough of a metal or mineral to make extraction economically worthwhile.
Continuous process by which rocks form, break down and re-form as igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock.
Breakdown of rock where it is, by physical, chemical or biological processes.
Removal and transport of rock fragments by water, wind or ice.
Rock and soil lying on top of a mineral deposit that must be removed in surface mining.
Waste rock from mining, piled up near the mine.
Surface mining: removing overburden to dig out a deposit near the surface.
Reaching deep deposits through vertical shafts and tunnels.
Environmental impact assessment: study of a project’s likely impacts before it is approved.
Returning a mined site to a useful state: filling, landscaping, replacing topsoil, planting.
A resource that exists in limited amounts and will run out.
Energy from a source that will not run out, e.g. wind, solar, HEP, tidal, geothermal.
Energy from a source that will run out, e.g. coal, oil, natural gas, uranium.
Coal, oil or natural gas, formed from remains of organisms over millions of years.
Fuel made from plant material or animal waste, e.g. ethanol from sugar cane.
Getting the same result using less energy, e.g. LED bulbs, insulation.
Meeting the needs of people today without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

examIntro: Paper 1 Section A style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme. Your mine case study answers go in the last box: fill it in once so it is ready to learn.

exam.q: Describe how sedimentary rocks are formed.
points: Rocks are weathered and eroded into small pieces (sediment)
Sediment is transported and deposited in layers, often under water
Layers are compacted by the weight of layers above
Particles are cemented together over a long time

exam.q: Explain why a mining company might decide not to extract a mineral deposit.
points: Ore grade is too low
Deposit is too deep, so extraction costs too much
World price or demand for the mineral is low
Poor transport links / remote location
The area is protected or environmental laws are strict
Local opposition
exam.note: Any 3. “Explain” means each point needs a reason, e.g. low grade means little profit.

exam.q: Describe how a mine site can be restored when mining ends.
points: Fill the pit with overburden or waste rock
Landscape the land to a natural shape
Replace topsoil and add fertiliser
Plant trees and other vegetation
Flood the pit to make a lake for wildlife or recreation
Monitor water for pollution

exam.q: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of nuclear power.
points: Adv: very low carbon dioxide emissions when generating
Adv: large amount of electricity from a small amount of fuel
Adv: reliable supply, not dependent on weather
Disadv: radioactive waste stays dangerous for thousands of years
Disadv: risk of accidents releasing radiation
Disadv: very expensive to build and decommission

exam.q: Suggest three ways a household could reduce its use of energy.
points: Insulate the loft / walls; fit double glazing
Use LED or energy-efficient bulbs
Buy energy-efficient appliances
Switch off devices instead of leaving them on standby
Install solar panels or solar water heating
Walk, cycle or use public transport

exam.q: For a mine you have studied: name it and its country, then describe its impacts and how it was managed.
points: Name and location (country, region)
What is mined and how (open-pit or shaft)
One or two environmental impacts, with detail
One or two social or economic impacts (jobs, displacement)
How it was managed or restored
A specific fact or figure that shows you know this mine
